quiz.title: Chapter 17 Quiz: Research for Legal Scholarship
quiz.intro: Ten questions on finding a topic, preemption checking, and writing the paper one question at a time.

items.q: What do all the shapes of a scholarly paper the chapter describes have in common?
options: They all argue a circuit split
The topic resolves into a question, and the thesis is the answer the paper defends
They all begin with a case comment
items.why: Unsettled question, live controversy, system that needs fixing, synthesis, response to a new opinion: every version ends the same way (Finding a Topic).

options: The questions earlier reading left open (issues reserved, points flagged beyond scope, disputes never engaged), collected as you go
A database of law review titles
items.why: A well-fed inventory means you may never face the blank page (Finding a Topic).

items.q: The four things to ask of a candidate topic are whether it is:
options: Supportable, open or fixable, worth answering, and something you can live with for a semester
items.why: And be realistic about scope: a narrow question answered thoroughly is a contribution (Finding a Topic).

items.q: The cursory preemption check should take:
options: About an hour, searching the claim’s distinctive terms in HeinOnline, Westlaw or Lexis, SSRN, and Google Scholar
items.why: If someone has written your paper, you want to know before the outline exists (Mapping the Scholarly Landscape).

options: Checking whether your argument has already been made
items.why: A different use of the word from Chapters 1 and 6 (Conducting preemption research).

items.q: An article in the same area as yours is:
options: Not preemption; an article making your argument is
A reason to abandon the topic
items.why: Read for the thesis, not the topic; then differentiate or pivot (the protocol, Step 2).

items.q: The chapter says most scholarly papers answer a short sequence of questions:
options: What is the framework; what problem has emerged; why the framework fails; what should be done; and what the strongest objection is
items.why: Each section exists to answer one big question, which breaks into research questions (Writing the Paper One Question at a Time).

items.q: The chapter recommends drafting the outline as:
options: Questions, because a question can be answered and answered means done
items.why: Not “III. The DMCA framework” but “III. What does the DMCA’s takedown process actually require?” (Writing the Paper One Question at a Time).

items.q: The caution about SSRN working papers is that they:
options: Have not been peer-reviewed and may change before publication, so rely on them with that caveat
items.why: SSRN puts you at the front of the conversation (SSRN and Working Papers; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: “AI and copyright” is, in the chapter’s terms:
options: A shelf: a subject area to browse, not a question a paper can answer
items.why: A subject area is a shelf to browse, not a paper to write (Common Pitfalls; Exercise 17.1).

drills.title: Shelf or Question?
drills.blurb: Eight candidates. A subject area to browse, a question a paper could answer, or an entry someone else’s text left open?

drills.title: The Scholarship Sequence
drills.blurb: From the question inventory to the final preemption sweep. Put the stages of a paper in order.
